item.title: Microsoft outage cut email and Teams across Europe, disrupting UK health appointments and schools
item.description: Microsoft says the fault came from a network change it has now reversed, and that there was no sign of malicious activity. Nicky Stewart warned the disruption shows the cost of relying on a single cloud provider.

item.title: Japan to raise income tax from 2027 to fund defence build-up
item.description: The government and ruling coalition decided on 18 December to lift the tax in January 2027, while cutting the Reconstruction Special Income Tax by one point. On a single-year basis, the tax burden would not increase for the time being.

item.title: Analyst says Ukrainian strikes put about 55% of Russia's petrol refining out of action
item.description: Debris from the same night's drone attack left 114 apartment buildings in Rostov-on-Don without heating, and Rosneft has reinstated fuel sales limits as queues form at petrol stations in Volgograd.

item.title: Quantum Systems drone fleet flying again after cyberattack on update server
item.description: The Bundeswehr had grounded a large share of the fleet as a precaution, the Financial Times reported, and federal authorities are investigating the attack that Der Spiegel reported reached Bundeswehr servers before anyone detected it.

item.title: Slovakia and France team up to push for power bills decoupled from gas prices
item.description: President Peter Pellegrini called the EU's gas-linked pricing illogical for a country that does not depend on gas for its electricity. The visit also brought a 120 million euro helicopter deal and talks on defence cooperation.

item.title: Nordic ministers to develop joint defence agreement as Sweden borrows SEK 300bn
item.description: The planned agreement would give Nordic defence cooperation a legal footing, while DN reports Sweden's record defence funding still falls short of Nato targets. From 1 January 2027, conscripts up to 47 can be called back for standby or war service.

item.title: Guterres urges windfall tax on oil giants, cites $600 million climate fund
item.description: The UN Secretary-General told COP31 leaders that nine oil companies made $95 billion in profits last quarter, while the Loss and Damage Fund has received $600 million. He said it is time to make polluters pay.

item.title: Europe guards its ministries and leaves its food to hackers
item.description: The state intercepted 3.5 million malicious emails for the foreign ministry while supermarkets were broken into through open doors the government itself named. We pay twice, in spoiled food and in fear.

item.title: Up to 50 leaders join Rutte in Dublin in Garda's biggest operation, say Gardaí
item.description: More than 5,000 Gardaí will work over 15,000 twelve-hour tours for the summit, while protesters march on Friday over fuel prices and the cost of living.

item.title: British police arrest serving US soldier on suspicion of spying for Russia
item.description: The 41-year-old was held under the National Security Act near Nato's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps headquarters in Gloucestershire, and faces possible charges from both Britain and the US Army.

item.title: EU and investors pledge over €10 billion to help European tech firms grow global
item.description: The EIB Group, 15 institutional investors and seven member states have pledged over €10 billion and hope to mobilise up to €80 billion in total, from a first closing of around €2 billion. The money is a pledge, not cash, and the European Commission calculated EU venture funding was about 84 percent below the American level in 2024.

item.title: Italy to give Zelensky's troops access to its radar satellites in thirteenth aid package
item.description: Defence Minister Guido Crosetto will present the package to the security committee Copasir on 10 November and propose extending arms supplies into 2027, as Salvini proposes halting arms and money for Ukraine.

item.title: Hungarian media report Viktor Orbán's brother Áron detained in visa fraud raids
item.description: Four people were held in Budapest, Fót and Dunakeszi over a scheme that charged Vietnamese citizens recruitment fees for visas to reach Western Europe. Viktor Orbán called the investigation a witch-hunt against him.

item.title: Republican Massie files eight impeachment articles against Defense Secretary Hegseth
item.description: The Kentucky congressman accuses Hegseth of waging war on Iran without Congress's approval and of unlawful strikes he says killed hundreds of civilians. House Speaker Mike Johnson calls the move a political trick.

item.title: Europe set to be left out of the room as Russia and Ukraine meet in Abu Dhabi
item.description: Kaja Kallas warns the EU will not implement any deal it is not part of, and the row over representation now goes on the agenda when EU leaders meet on 13 November.

item.title: At least 20 dead in two boats off Crete, two still missing
item.description: The Greek coastguard arrested two suspected smugglers after a dinghy was found in distress south of Kali Limenes. Deputy minister Sevi Voloudaki says Minister Pleuris will announce within days a plan for return hubs outside Europe's territory.

item.title: Ten northern navies to sign North Atlantic pact without the US
item.description: The ten Joint Expeditionary Force countries, put forward by Norway, will share doctrine, training, equipment and ammunition under the Royal Navy's Maritime Proposition, after Washington told allies in July it would cut its NATO fighter aircraft by a third.

item.title: Voters punished the man who taxed their prices. Europe must answer tariffs with one voice
item.description: Section 301 lets the US president tax European trade with no vote by lawmakers, and the election changed nothing about that power. Every government that cuts its own deal spends the strongest card Europe holds.

item.title: Meta, Google and TikTok sue to block California ban on addictive feeds for under-16s
item.description: The companies filed suit on November 4 against Assembly Bill 1709, which they call a violation of free speech. Attorney General Rob Bonta's office says it will defend the law in court.

item.title: Belgrade judge detains special police commander on torture suspicion
item.description: The head of Serbia's SAJ unit faces up to 30 days in detention over the alleged torture of ten people in a government garage. The Belgrade Bar Association says the timing of arrests at the close of the election campaign raises suspicion of political use of police and prosecutors.

item.title: House vote looms on impeaching US defence secretary Pete Hegseth over Iran war
item.description: Representative Thomas Massie plans to force the vote next week, and President Trump says he intends to keep his defence secretary. The war has cost $47 billion.

item.title: Iraq proposes ministerial shuttle between Tehran and Washington as losses pass $60bn
item.description: Oil revenues lost since February 2026 equal about €54 billion, and oil funds roughly 90 percent of the federal budget. Foreign minister Fuad Hussein's plan follows Iranian terms for resuming talks, including reopening the Strait of Hormuz.

item.title: Six Nordic defence firms propose shared missile warning and Arctic surveillance
item.description: The Nordic Compass statement, led by former Finnish Prime Minister Jyrki Katainen, also sets out four steps towards one Nordic defence market. Governments of the five Nordic countries are invited to join.

item.title: Parliament to debate EU cybersecurity plan for hospitals, schools and power grids
item.description: The debate on 11 November follows a January Commission proposal to tighten the union's ICT supply chains and give ENISA a stronger role. No step in the procedure has yet been recorded.

item.title: EU picks Proximus and three other suppliers for six-year sovereign cloud contract
item.description: The Belgian state still owns 53% of Proximus. The framework deal covers the Commission, Parliament, Council and 70 agencies.

item.title: Brussels found the addiction. Now it must ban the design, not the bans.
item.description: The Commission's own findings name the machinery of Meta's and TikTok's addictive design, yet after two years and five sets of findings there is no final decision and no scroll switched off. With lawmakers in seven countries moving to ban infinite scroll, autoplay and luring notifications, the Commission should write the ban Europe-wide into the Digital Fairness Act instead of calling the patchwork fragmentation.
